newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - DSM earnings drop, shares slip.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - DSM earnings drop, shares slip.

text.p: Dutch petrochemicals group DSM NV reported lower than expected third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, hit by a squeeze on margins which it expected to continue into the fourth quarter.
Net profit fell to 178 million guilders ($104 million) from 234 million a year earlier. Analysts had been expecting a net profit of between 181 and 212 million guilders.
DSM said earnings were squeezed at both ends by lower prices for its products and higher costs for its raw materials, which led to narrower profit margins.
"This (lower profit) was mainly due to lower margins caused on the one hand by lower prices and on the other by higher feedstock costs, especially for naphtha," it said.
Fourth-quarter results would also be affected adversely by higher feedstock costs, particularly for naphtha, the main raw material for the petrochemicals and plastics industries, DSM said.
But it said it was maintaining its previous forecast that 1996 would be a good year.
Investors appeared unconvinced, with DSM shares among the biggest losers on a falling Amsterdam bourse, shedding 6.80 guilders or a hefty four percent to 159.80 at one point.

Analysts said operating profits were sharply lower than expected at 239 million guilders, versus a year-earlier 342 million, although the bottom-line impact had been limited by a lower tax bill and interest charges.
"Net profits were only slightly lower than...we were expecting but the quality of earnings has deteriorated," said Bert Schouten, chemicals analyst with merchant bank MeesPierson.
"Obviously margins on hydrocarbons and polymers were even narrower than expected," said Nils van Elzelingen of brokers NIB Strating.
Schouten said the continuing rise in the price of naphtha could have a substantial impact on DSM's fourth-quarter performance.
Higher prices and a stronger dollar have left DSM facing naphtha costs that are around 30 percent higher than in the first quarter.
DSM said earlier it would only be possible to pass on a part of the increase in feedstock costs in its product prices.
Analysts said that after the third-quarter results, they were weighing a reduction in full-year earnings per share estimates although their ratings of the stock would remain unchanged.
